title: Introducing the Model Assistant: from ‘what if’ to modelled insight
gist: Oxford Economics launched the AskOEAI Model Assistant, a conversational AI add-on to its Global Economic Model (GEM) that turns plain-language 'what if' prompts into research-calibrated shocks and runs full GEM simulations benchmarked to its baseline. The pitch is that, unlike general-purpose chatbots, the numbers come from a validated model rather than LLM narrative, though bespoke stress tests still need human calibration.

insights.claim: Building credible macro scenarios has been bottlenecked by three skills: knowing which of a large model's thousands of variables are the key levers, sizing and timing the shock from historical research, and setting up, solving and interpreting the model.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Explains why investment teams historically ran few scenarios; lowering this barrier raises the volume of stress tests analysts can run.
insights.quote: Our Global Economic Model (GEM) contains thousands of variables, but a subset of these are the key ones to generate complete economic scenarios with full transmissions.

insights.claim: According to Oxford Economics, even experienced macro modellers spend much of their time identifying indicators and building inputs before analysis starts, which caps the number of scenarios they can explore.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Automation of input-building is where AI may give the biggest productivity gain in macro research workflows.
insights.quote: Even experienced modellers can spend much of their time identifying the right indicators and building inputs before any analysis begins

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' AskOEAI Model Assistant, billed as the world's first AI assistant for scenario modelling, runs a four-step workflow: describe the scenario in plain language, have the assistant research and propose shocks with rationales, review inputs against the baseline, then analyse results and re-solve.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Signals incumbent macro-data vendors embedding agentic AI directly into their proprietary models as a product moat.
insights.quote: The Model Assistant is the world’s first AI assistant for scenario modelling.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics says the Model Assistant calibrates shock size and timing from the firm's own published research, such as an existing downside case for a prolonged conflict or trade war, supplemented by verified external sources.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Scenario outputs will inherit the house view's priors, so users should know they are getting Oxford Economics' calibration, not a neutral one.
insights.quote: If our economists have published a downside case for a prolonged conflict or a trade war, that becomes the starting point for the size and timing of the inputs

insights.claim: Oxford Economics says the Model Assistant does not itself generate results; it sends structured inputs to the GEM and runs a full simulation using the same model its economists use for forecasts, benchmarked against the latest baseline.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Separating the LLM interface from the numerical engine is the design pattern that makes AI outputs auditable for investment use.
insights.quote: Critically the assistant does not generate the results, it sends structured inputs to the GEM and runs a full simulation

insights.claim: Oxford Economics argues general-purpose AI tools give plausible-sounding economic answers, for example on Middle East escalation and bond yields, but their numbers are not produced by a validated model and their assumptions are hard to trace.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Cautions investors against relying on chatbot macro estimates; the value of proprietary validated models persists in the AI era.
insights.quote: But the numbers are not produced by a validated economic model and the assumptions are hard to trace.
insights.locator: Why it is more than a chatbot

insights.claim: The Model Assistant embeds modellers' knowledge of which GEM indicators actually transmit through the model, steering users away from shocking variables that do not meaningfully feed through.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Domain-specific guardrails, not raw LLM capability, are the vendor's claimed edge over generic AI.
insights.quote: If you try to shock a variable that does not meaningfully feed through the model, it steers you towards a better option.
insights.locator: Trained on how the GEM works.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics targets the Model Assistant at non-modellers such as risk managers, investment analysts, portfolio teams and consultants, and at existing GEM users who want a first-draft scenario in minutes.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Broadens the addressable user base for macro-model subscriptions beyond specialist economists.
insights.quote: the assistant produces a first-draft scenario in minutes, making it easy to test multiple shocks
insights.locator: The second is existing GEM users

insights.claim: Oxford Economics concedes the Model Assistant suits high-level narrative scenarios, while complex bespoke work such as regulatory stress tests or detailed geopolitical scenarios needing client-specific calibration still requires tailored human work.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: AI-driven scenarios are a screening tool, not a substitute for calibrated stress tests in regulated risk processes.
insights.quote: Complex bespoke exercises, such as regulatory stress tests or detailed geopolitical scenarios that need client-specific calibration, still benefit from tailored work

insights.claim: Oxford Economics notes that a question many of its clients are asking now is what a renewed escalation of the war in Iran would mean for the global economy and government bond yields, which it uses as the showcase for the Model Assistant.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Signals that Iran-war escalation and its rates impact is a top-of-mind client risk scenario.
insights.quote: what would a renewed escalation of the war in Iran mean for the global economy and for government bond yields?
